chapter: Erroll Garner, the 1952 arrest and Florida
title: Clifford Brown and the young geniuses who died early
summary: He heard Clifford Brown practicing between sets in Miami; reflects that geniuses die young.

bands.name: Chris Powell and His Blue Flames

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Trumpeters I admired: rating the horn players

blocks.x: Mother Kelly's. That's right. I'm sorry. Out of Chicago. And we moved into the Riviera. Well, the band that we followed in there was Chris [Columbus]* and His Blue Flames, and that's where I met Clifford Brown. He was working with Chris Columbus. And Clifford wasn't a great person at that time. He was back in the back, trying to get his fingers together and passages together and everything. He was blowing on his horn between intermission all the time he was on intermission and go right back like we'd never had intermission, you know. Horn constantly in his mouth. And when he got himself together, he got himself together. Once he broke out. And his mouth, visually, it didn't appear as though he should play a trumpet. His lips looked like they were more suitable to play a trombone than a trumpet, you know. They were sort of on the thick side, you know. But he got those notes out of that trumpet. He just manhandled it, you know. Play fast as lightening. No technique, but he played from his soul. And they say geniuses die young, so I know I'm not a genius, thank God. And it's rang pretty true, because all those youngsters that I recall, like Jimmy Blanton, died young. Bud Powell died fairly young. And who else?
